utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I only notice the absence of Mr. Meek. The Prosecution is just Mr. McCloskey today. Mr. Butler, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to proceed with Mr. Bourgon's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Judges. Good afternoon, colleagues. Good afternoon, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When we left off yesterday, we were in the Brigade Rules which is 65 ter number 694, and we were looking at -- at least I was hoping to look at paragraph 208 of this publication, which is in English on page 61, and B/C/S, page 99. Can I have this on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My aim in showing you this document, Mr. Butler, was to -- as we were exploring the avenue or the differences between the intelligence officer and the assistant commander for security, and we were looking at different tasks which are performed by the intelligence officer in support of combat activities. And we were looking at paragraph 208, which mentioned that the intelligence officer would use the intelligence -- process and use intelligence about the enemy, the area of combat operations, and weather conditions in the zone of intelligence responsibility. Do you see this in paragraph 208?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, yes, in 208 it talks about the purposes of intelligence support. It doesn't particularly name an intelligence officer, but obviously the intelligence officer would be behind this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at the end of this paragraph, of course we see that the focus in wartime must be on gathering data relevant for making decisions for the deployment of forces. And I take it you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And we also are looking at paragraph 209, which also highlights what the intelligent officer does, and where it is mentioned that he actually carries out intelligence support tasks, and that within the brigade, there would be a plan for gathering the data, and that this plan would be drafted by the intelligence organ. Does that correspond to your understanding of the intelligence officer within the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again, it describes what the intelligence organ is required to do, and then obviously the intelligence officer is responsible for the implementation of that, although, again as it notes, the brigade commander is ultimately the person responsible for the organisation of intelligence support.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it is my understanding that in preparing your VRS brigade command responsibility report, you would have studied these brigade rules, especially with regards to the intelligence officer and the assistant commander for security, in order to be able to tell the difference between the two. Is that what you did?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily tell the difference between the two, but certainly to understand the difference in functions between the two services, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in light of these duties and responsibilities of the intelligence officer, I take it you will agree with me that this officer works, of course, in the Operations Department of the Command Staff, that he is involved in the planning of operations, and if there's someone in the brigade, after of course the chief of staff and the commander, who is aware of what is going on on the operations side, it would be the intelligence officer. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after the commander and chief of staff, the next person who would have the broadest view of what was going on would be the chief of operations. Obviously, the chief of intelligence, who's required to support that operational process, should have, you know, at least an equal view of what the proposed operation is in order to be able to properly support it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, using the example of the information which was apparently available to the Main Staff, the Drina Corps Command, concerning the column, and I take it you describe or you label this information as being inaccurate, or at least in the beginning, would you agree with me that incorrect intelligence, inaccurate intelligence, or late information can have disastrous consequences for the successful conduct of combat activities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and, you know, perhaps going back to the paragraph 208 from the intelligence manual we were looking at yesterday, it specifically reflects the issue of having to deal with inaccurate, incomplete, or late intelligence information and the ramifications on combat. So, yes, not having an accurate intelligence picture, or having an accurate intelligence picture too late, certainly will adversely impact a military commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, I don't mean to interrupt you, but do you think we really need a military expert to tell us something like what we have just heard?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Butler has been labelled as an intelligence analyst, and if I want to highlight the duties and responsibilities of the assistant command for security, I feel it is of a necessity to first highlight what is intelligence, what intelligence does, and then I move to the assistant commander for security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Turning to counter-intelligence, Mr. Butler, you will agree with me that although counter-intelligence also deals with information, it is an entirely different domain; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The domain of counter-intelligence, while it may include the actual collection of intelligence-related information, the overall purpose behind counter-intelligence is to deny what are known as essential elements of friendly information to a potential enemy force.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you will agree that the aim of counter-intelligence, and I use your words, to deny the enemy's intelligence-gathering function, and in doing so to protect all of the information -- information, sorry, which would be available and circulating within the brigade, the brigade command and the brigade subordinate units; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, within the general purview of every officer's and unit's responsibility to take basic security measures, that is one part of denying information to a potential enemy. The role of counter-intelligence, in large part, deals with those issues that are normally beyond the purview of basic security functions that a unit would do. So, again, it's all within the same role, although different manners of how it's accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So would you agree that counter-intelligence includes the following, and you can answer by "yes" or "no" unless you wish to elaborate, that counter-intelligence includes: The evaluation of manifested and expected intelligence gathering activity and other subversive activity of the enemy? Is that one of the things that counter-intelligence does?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counter-intelligence does, in fact, evaluate the anticipated subversive activity of the enemy. Again like all other forms of collecting information, it evaluates it with respect to determine accuracy, validity, and then in a military context, to predict forward what that threat will be in the future to allow a commander to deal with it. So, I mean, yes, they do evaluate information, but they don't evaluate it in the same manner that traditional tactical intelligence would be evaluated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this includes the detection and prevention of hostile activities by individual groups or organisations against the brigade and members of the brigade; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the respect that we're defining "hostile actions" to not necessarily be military attacks but would include a larger body of things such as subversion directed against the authority of commanders or of actual military discipline, things of that nature, so it's much broader than just the phrase "a military hostile threat."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank you for this. It's an important clarification. Now, with respect to enemy, if we consider any relationship between the assistant commander for security and the enemy, his focus would have to be on special forces elements which, of course, may be infiltrated in friendly territory; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be one aim that he would be looking for is in an effort to collect information that could be used to prevent that type of infiltration. That's one of his aims, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in performing his counter-intelligence duties, there are many things which the assistant commander for security can and may do. One example would be dealing with secret sources of information. I'll give you a few examples: Informants, secret collaborators, or any other person willing to provide information. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That falls under his -- what are described as his operative tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And he may do some -- he may also use some technical means, such as wiretapping, for example, or he can also be controlling incoming and outgoing mail?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly with the issue of wiretapping or monitoring the brigade's communications as a way of trying to evaluate whether information is being -- is leaving the brigade from that way would be within his purview. Mail -- the controlling of mail -- and I assume when we're talking about mail, we're talking about soldiers' mail and things of that nature. I mean, in that regard it would potentially be a function to ensure that soldiers either are, by design or, you know, inadvertently, are making, you know -- putting stuff in letters and things back to family members which could be potentially used to compromise future plans, operations, or capabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, one of the other things that the assistant commander for security does is he may be investigating persons who may present, in his view, a threat to the security of information within the brigade? Is that something that he would do?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that would fall into one of his functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when he does all these functions, the assistant commander for security, I mean, his work, would you agree with me, is quite different from that of the intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, sir, I mean, the tasks that you have essentially described are those same tasks that we saw in the October 1994 memo from General Mladic, which reflect that they want their security officers to be performing 80 per cent of these types of functions -- or these types of functions as 80 per cent of their time. Most of these functions are outside of the normal role of what an intelligence officer would be expected to perform as part of their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And within the Zvornik Brigade, you've already testified to this, that the intelligence and the security functions were managed by two different branches, where you had the assistant commander for security was Drago Nikolic, and the intelligence officer was the -- or assistant chief of staff for intelligence was Dusko Vukotic. That's in accordance with the information that you have; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's what I understand for July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you've also described, looking at one of the documents which was shown to you, that this situation is different from the what it was in a light infantry brigade, at least before January of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in January of 1995, there was an instruction which was published which even in a light infantry brigade, the two tasks were separated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct, at least in theory and practical reality, to the best degree possible, given the shortage of qualified officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I look at -- just so that we understand by what is a light infantry brigade, it would be much smaller and a much simpler structure and would use light weaponry which would enable it to carry out combat tasks with a greater degree of independence; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. I would categorise the difference between a standard infantry brigade and a light infantry brigade along the lines of a standard infantry brigade, while having more people, would also have a wider variety of either heavier forces with respect to motorised forces, a motorised company, an armoured company, more heavy mechanised tools of warfare than a traditional light infantry brigade. Each has its place on the battlefield. A heavier infantry brigade or a standard infantry brigade has more combat power to achieve particular objectives. A light infantry brigade has less combat power, but because of its mobility can operate in areas of the battlefield that a heavier unit may not be able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now that's probably why, in a light infantry brigade in the beginning or within the JNA doctrine, they tried to have less people as possible within the command and they say maybe intelligence and security can be doubled up into the same person; would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I mean within the context of the JNA it does reflect a smaller structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I suggest to you that the reason why, in January of 1995, when they decided to split the two functions for all brigades within the VRS, this was because, simply, the two functions is too much for one person; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, given -- given the orders and memos with respect to the security branches that came out in late 1994, I believe it is fair to conclude that there was a recognition on the part of the military leadership that at some point, because of competing requirements, that until this individual -- these tasks were split between different people, one of the particular tasks would suffer. And in this case, it appeared that the security tasks suffered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's why they -- there was this instruction by the Main Staff, which we referred to yesterday, 65 ter number 2741, which says -- talks about the 80 per cent which would be devoted to tasks of security; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in part. That particular memo is less with respect to active intelligence collection, but also defines the fact that the -- that within the role of security, you know, you have your strictly counter-intelligence and operative tasks, but also the fact that within the doctrine of the JNA and adopted by the VRS, security also included a law enforcement or crime prevention avenue that had to also be undertaken. And I think what that particular issue revolved around was the fact that more and more security officers were getting detailed to spend more time doing crime prevention work as opposed to doing strictly security organ work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if we look at whether it is from the security rules, the document we looked at yesterday, or within the document which you have not considered, the means and methods for security officers, would you agree with me that that 80 per cent that they were focusing on in that Main Staff instruction was 80 per cent for counter-intelligence solely?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which document didn't -- I not consider? We're talking about this document -- the document that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The means and methods of security. You told us yesterday that it was too low or too technical of a manual for you to consider in making your VRS command responsibility report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I didn't say that I didn't consider it, because I did in fact review it. What I said was that given the technical issue related to it, and -- there was not anything relevant in that particular manual dealing with the context of the report that I needed and what I was looking for. So, I mean, I did review it, and, you know, where applicable in my analysis, I considered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My point is just I'm trying to get back to the answer you just gave concerning the law enforcement and crime prevention. You called it, at page 10, lines 20: "... Crime prevention work, as opposed to doing strictly security organ work"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, the VRS wanted to stress the counter-intelligence work and de-emphasise the time that security officers spent on crime prevention, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that crime prevention is not included in the 80 per cent they were looking for? That's my point.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the context that they're talking about, while crime is obviously a security issue, I would agree with that. Crime prevention, per se, does not fall within that 80 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During your examination-in-chief, you testified about paragraph 4 of the January order. Maybe we can take this one up. It's 3031. If we can have this in e-court, please. And I take it you have a binder beside you, and Mr. Butler if you can look at tab 26. And that was at page 19648, lines 8 to 13, where you provided some information concerning paragraph 4, which reads as follows: "Security organs and intelligence organs shall exchange the information of importance on a daily basis." You stated during your testimony that this recognised the fact that some information obtained through intelligence channels may have importance to maintaining the overall security posture of the unit, and that some information obtained through security channels may have intelligence value. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you would agree that the information which will be shared between the intelligence function and the security organ, this will not be all the information which they gather in their respective organ, but rather the information that is important for the other?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would think that the flow of information from the intelligence to the security organ would probably be more comprehensive than the flow of information from the security organ to the intelligence organ in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you would not expect, based on your own experience, to see the intelligence officer sharing all of the information in his possession concerning the upcoming combat activities, for example?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- like I said, I would disagree with that, because I would think that with respect to intelligence, the security officer, as a function of being able to perform his job, has to have a very detailed view of the incoming intelligence, particularly with respect to an operational nature, as we've discussed, with the issue relating to diversionary units or potential issues of sabotage or things like that. So certainly in the abstract that the intelligence officer might withhold information that he deems the security officer would not have a professional interest in. As I said before, I mean, in practice, if the flow of information going from the intelligence officer to the security officer would probably be much wider than going the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Much wider, but my point is, for example, if the intelligence officer has information on special forces of the enemy, of course that would be of interest to the security officer, but overall information concerning enemy activities, he would not share unless he be requested to do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Asked and answered. We're getting into the abstract upon abstract.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I quite agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll go on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Moving on to the management of the security organ, this is a topic that was covered during your examination-in-chief and that you also covered in your report at paragraph 3.13. I'm talking about the VRS command responsibility report. And you've confirmed already, I take it, that the assistant commander for security is the directly subordinated to the brigade commander, as confirmed by the rules.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir. I mean, we're talking, again in this case, within the command sense, he is a superior officer in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now nonetheless, pursuant to paragraph 18 of the rules, where we know that the security organ of the Drina Corps provides specialist administrative services for the brigade assistant commander for security, and he provides also assistance to that organ, you've testified about that in your examination-in-chief; do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's the management or technical chain that exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's at page 19646, line 1 to 16, and you define this relationship as being a technical or management chain that runs along but certainly does not supersede the command chain?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this issue itself was not included in your VRS command responsibility report, was it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The issue of the technical management.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was discussed in some degree in the brigade command report with respect to the roles and responsibilities of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, I won't -- I won't question you, but I believe it wasn't, and I'll move on to another topic. Now, when I look at the way you describe this technical or management chain, I'd like you to use an example for you to confirm how this works within the brigade. And I take it you're familiar with the fact that security officers or the assistant commander for security was not supposed to be on duty, to perform the duty of operations duty officer. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware, particularly, you know, with respect to the Zvornik Brigade, that that was an issue of whether or not the assistant commander of security could be used for non-security functions such as being a duty officer, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. You're aware of an issue, but are you aware of the rule that the assistant commander for security is not supposed to be -- to perform brigade operations duty?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I'm aware of that as a VRS rule. I don't recall ever seeing that in any document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have 65 ter 407, which is the rules on security, and I have paragraph 93, page 32 in English and page 26 in B/C/S. If I can have this in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 93, at the last part of this paragraph, can you read this and say whether this confirms that the security officer or the assistant commander for security was not supposed to be or to perform the duty of operations duty officer? The last part.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just trying to figure out -- within the context, it's kind of tough to figure out what the phrase "in the interior service." I can see --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If you're not familiar with this fact, I mean, as I say we can move on.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I say, it may well have been within the JNA context, that was it. I just -- if we read "interior service," to be within, you know, a traditional military unit, then that rule would be in place within the JNA, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, on this basis, you know that when this issue came up about whether a security officer -- what the role and duties of the security officer were to be, that at a certain point in time the commander of the Zvornik Brigade imposed some new modus operandi on the assistant commander for security with respect to handling of the mail, with respect to being on duty, and with respect to the car being put at his disposal. Is that something that was -- that came out in your analysis of the facts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, primarily because the information that -- that was derived from was almost exclusively witness based. So although I'm aware of it with respect to the construction of my reports, it's not reflected as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But Is that an issue you came across when you did your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Specifically with respect to Zvornik, I'm aware that there was a -- there was an issue with respect to the roles of the security officer within the larger context of the command and staff, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when the Main Staff instruction was issued, that was in October of 1994, are you aware that the situation was almost put back to the way it was before those problems came out? Is that something that was revealed by your investigation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of it from -- from the testimony of other individuals. I mean, I don't think that that was a subject of investigation, per se.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then did you explore, while you were analysing the facts of this case, did you explore the issue that the only officer within the -- the only assistant commander for security within the Drina Corps who was doing -- performing duties as operations duty officer was Drago Nikolic? Is that something that you looked into?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is that a fact -- is that something that could influence or have an impact on the manner and the availability of the assistant commander for security to perform his duties?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would presumably, in abstract, be a factor. But within the context of my analysis, it wouldn't be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, as I've just mentioned, when the Main Staff instruction was issued, Drago Nikolic was given back his mail rights, if I can use this term, and also a better use of the car put at his disposal. However, he was -- he remained as somebody who was called upon to preform the duties of brigade operations officer. Are you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that while he was given back those -- his car and the ability to pass, you know, mail in a separate channel, that he was still required to perform his functions as a duty officer, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, just to clarify, I think you meant "brigade duty operations officer," not "operations officer."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank my colleague. I was talking about duty operations officer, and I may have used this wrong term earlier, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may have, actually. You did use it correctly earlier on, but I think in the interim you did make the same mistake. Go ahead. It will be corrected, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, if this was contrary to the rules for Drago Nikolic to be called upon to perform the duties of brigade duty operations officer, what could he do about it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a practical sense within the structure at the time, he had a course of recourse, which would be to complain about that to his immediate superior within the technical chain, which would be Colonel Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then what could Colonel Popovic do about it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Popovic would either make a decision to take that to the corps commander, who could then potentially direct Colonel Pandurevic to rescind the order, Colonel Popovic could take that up to the Main Staff security and intelligence sector, which would then presumably send an order to the Drina Corps commander to instruct the brigade commander to rescind that, or he could do nothing and learn to live with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my interest here is to -- is whether you would agree with me that the only one who could actually order the brigade commander to change this would be his immediate superior, the corps commander. Would you agree with that? Or a higher level, but at least at the corps level, Colonel Popovic could not give that order to the brigade commander, the only one that could do that was the corps commander, Krstic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time we're talking about Zivanovic, but, yes, that would be the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that is a fair illustration of the unity of command principal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the separation of authorities between command and technical management, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's exactly my point, that this shows that technical management is not a command authority in any way. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, any command authority that -- that might be implied, it would be, in effect, derived from the authorities provided by the commander, not inherent within their own position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on to the authority over the military police, also an issue that was discussed during your examination-in-chief. And we've already -- I've already asked you this question. You confirmed that the commander of the military police, the first commander was Jasikovac, who was the commander of the military police company?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the immediate company commander in July of 1995, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And his immediate supervisor or superior, sorry, not supervisor, but his immediate superior, his commander, was the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Drago Nikolic did not exercise command over the military police?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Nonetheless, there is some kind of a relationship between the military police and the assistant commander for security?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that would be, for example, specialised -- I'm looking to the rules here, specialised management, recommending the use of the military police to the commander, and being responsible to the commander for the state of activity -- sorry, the state and the activity of the military police unit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure "state of activity" -- I mean, if you're referring to the state of training of the military police unit or something of that nature, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, in paragraph 3.15 of your report, you say that the assistant commander for security makes suggestions to the commander on the use of the military police?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is, by position, one of his functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And according to the rules, you would agree that the -- it says here that he would be responsible for the combat readiness of the military police. Do you agree with this term, "combat readiness"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with it in so much as it -- it means traditional military police tasks. I take -- you know, in fact in reality in the VRS, the military police were often not used on traditional police tasks but were, in fact, used on tasks that are traditionally used by infantry. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's why I'd like you to define and to explain the term "combat readiness." Even in your own military experience, the term "combat readiness" does not necessarily mean being ready for combat, but rather it means being ready to perform whatever your task is in a combat environment; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. I mean, obviously the criteria of combat readiness for an infantry unit and the tasks that it would be able to -- would need to perform would be different from that of a logistics unit or that of a police unit or -- you know, just go down the list. So the phrase "combat readiness," you know, means the ability of that unit to perform the tasks that it, by doctrine, is supposed to be able to perform in a combat environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if the brigade commander decides to use the military police company, or parts thereof, in combat, it is not Drago Nikolic who will tell him how they will perform combat activities; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, a -- how they will actually implement combat activities, like I said, if in an infantry role it wouldn't normally be the job of the security officer to do that. The unit would be resubordinated or attached to an infantry formation, and it would be the higher combat commander who would tell the military police, through their commander, you know, how to employ, how to organise, and what tasks needed to be accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in this regard, you will agree that the role of the assistant commander for security is rather to advise the commander as to whether it is appropriate at any given time to devote military police resources to combat rather than to their traditional role?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that would be something that the security officer would be obligated to raise to the commander as part of the performance of his duties, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And once the commander decides to use the military police, with or without the advice of the security officer, then that's it; he's the command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We salute and follow orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this can be confirmed, and I would ask you whether your analysis of the facts on the 12th, 13th and 14th of July, when military police resources were used by the chief of staff to fight the column, that this is an illustration that really Drago Nikolic had nothing to do in terms of where those military police would be used to fight or to defend against that column.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. With respect to the 12th and the 13th, at the time that the chief of staff decided that he was going to use the military police in a combat role, Drago Nikolic would -- there's no evidence that he was consulted on the best employment on terrain or other locations as a security officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, on the 12th of July, to be more precise, that's -- on that day, there was some elements of the military police were sent to Konjevic Polje to perform some traffic duties, and I take it that you will agree with me, based on your analysis of the facts, that they were sent there by Obrenovic without consulting Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly know that Obrenovic, as the chief of staff, gave the order. I have no way of knowing whether he did or did not consult with Drago Nikolic on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did your investigation or your analysis of the facts, of course based on your military experience, did that reveal that Drago Nikolic, on the 12th of July, was not present within the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 311 in e-court, please. And that's tab for you, Mr. Butler, in your binder -- that would be tab 28 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You're familiar with these kinds of reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we go to the line which refers to Drago Nikolic, and if you look under the date for the 12th of July -- it's on the second page, I'm sorry. Can I have the next page up, and it's number 38. And what does that show for the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The symbol is a "C."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And are you familiar with what was meant by the "C"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is usually a legend on these particular documents. I mean, I believe either that the "C" or the "O" symbol is often used to symbolise a day off, so to speak. You're not performing your military functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I agree with that, if that is the case, because I don't want you to say something that you don't know. But if that is the case, this report would confirm that Drago Nikolic was not there on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this would -- this report would be an indicator of that, yes, sir. I don't know that it would definitively confirm it, given the fact that orders were being given to ensure all units were at full combat readiness. I mean, the presumption is that somebody like the assistant commander for security is not going to be able to sit and enjoy his day off while the rest of the units were being told to bring all their other people in from leave. So I agree it's an indicator that he might not be there, but I can't say that definitively.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you agree with me that whenever you use these reports that talk about the presence or absence of the military police in any given place or date, that would also be an indicator and nothing else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is an indicator. I mean, I don't take it as a definitive fact, I mean. And given the fact that particularly in the military police log, you know, there has been evidence of altering, you know, I think that -- that's why.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to another topic, which is responsibility for prisoners of war. And I'd like to have in e-court 3D275. And I'd like to go to paragraph 134. The page in English is 39. I don't have the page in B/C/S. You would agree that, first of all, Mr. Butler, that while we wait for this to appear in e-court, that the security rules themselves, that's the document we were referring to earlier, 65 ter 407, are silent on the role of the security officer concerning prisoners of war, but admittedly you gave a reason for that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the issue of security officers and the prisoners of war, there is a role, but within the defined limits of what they're trying to accomplish; that is, trying to identify individuals who they could potentially cultivate as sources of information. That's within the limits of the JNA rules, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, with regards to military police themselves, and -- first, let's take this one. So we have this paragraph 134 here, and if you can say -- paragraph 134 of 3D275. That's the means and methods of the security organs, and this confirms, does it not, that prisoners of war, for the security officer, are but another source of information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they are a source of information. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in your report on the VRS command -- brigade command responsibility, at paragraph 3.19, you stated that at the brigade level, the commander was responsible for ensuring the proper interrogation of prisoners of war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'd have to show me that paragraph. I'd have to read it in context. "The proper interrogation of prisoners of war" sounds --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's your report. If we can go to that --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can look at the whole paragraph, maybe I can put it in context, because right now I'm not sure what that line in isolation is relevant to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: 65 ter 684 [Realtime transcript read in error "364"] in e-court, please, paragraph 3.19.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: 684. I'm sorry, the transcript indicates "364," but it's "684", sorry, "684". And the paragraph should be, in English, page 19, and also B/C/S, page 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't have this one in your binder, because it was too -- too many pages, but you can read from the screen that what you wrote is that: "At this level" --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That explains it. At the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Where it says: "At the brigade level ..." And in the middle of the paragraph, you're at the right page, 3.19?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There it is. Yes, sir. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This one, now we have the right page. And where it says in the middle: "At the brigade level, the brigade commander is responsible for ensuring the proper interrogation of prisoners of war, and of course through the intelligence organ"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the part that was left out of your initial phrase, and that's why I was kind of confused about that. I mean, obviously that is a responsibility exercised through his intelligence organ, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And so of course you would agree that the interrogation of prisoners of war as a - I was going to use "per se," but you're going to ask me to define "per se" - is more an intelligence function than a security function; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, for the immediate concerns of a brigade-level commander, the combat information that can be obtained from those types of individuals is of a priority to him. Obviously, while it's recognised that there will be a potentially longer-term intelligence collection effort, which may involve again the security officers trying to turn these people as potential long-term agents, a brigade commander, his primary goal is the tactical use of that information in order to increase his combat effectiveness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And just to finish with the brigade commander, if you read a little further down, you mention that at the same time he is also responsible to ensure that the provisions of the Geneva Conventions were strictly complied with in the treatment of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this paragraph, the meaning of this paragraph in your report, it was my understanding that you were trying to say that in the end, or the lower you get, the two functions, that of intelligence and security, kind of get closer together, because at the battalion level you only have one individual who does intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only is it reflected in the rules, but, yes, in the practical application, the lower that the echelons are, brigade or even corps, brigade, and battalion, you see a much more closer relationship between the intelligence and the security officers because the goals are different, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But the fact that the security and intelligence officer at the battalion level, because he's got two hats, has a primary responsibility for prisoners of war, that doesn't give any specific responsibility in that regard to the brigade assistant commander for security; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's fair, I mean, in the context where he would be functioning, you know, primarily as an intelligence officer pursuant to his -- the role of the responsibilities of his battalion commander, his activities related to dealing with prisoners of war would stay along that command chain. It wouldn't be a security issue, per se.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the military police, now that we've finished with the chain of command, if I can have 707 -- 65 ter 707 up on e-court, and I'd like to refer you to paragraphs 25(h) for "hotel," as well as paragraphs 55 and 57. Unfortunately, I don't have the page number. Maybe we can avoid looking at the document itself if you can confirm, Mr. Butler, that with respect to prisoners of war, according to these regulations, 707, those are the service regulations of the armed forces concerning the military police. And you said at the beginning of my cross-examination that you did refer to these -- these regulations, and that the role of military police, pursuant to the rules, is very limited concerning prisoners of war. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I would say it's very limited. The military police do have a role in issues related to prisoners of war, in so much as they are probably one of the primary means by which the commander will safeguard prisoners, keep them under appropriate guard, until such time that the prisoners keep them under appropriate guard until such time that the prisoners can be moved to the superior command or to an area, you know, designated by the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, is that based on your experience in the United States Army or in the VRS, based on the rules that you have there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that somewhere in the military police rules, it discusses that -- the fact that they do have a role in safeguarding the transport of prisoners, which would include prisoners of war. I think if you go up to 55, which is on the same page --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, paragraph 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, 55 talks about escorting persons under arrest who have committed a crime. Now, that's not a prisoner of war, is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but if you look at the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Prisoners of war and certain military property. And then that would go with paragraph 57, which says that they will escort prisoners of war, but that would be upon special order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So we cannot make a statement outright that the security of prisoners of war is a military police matter; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree. I think the regulations say that the military police have some competence in dealing with this issue, yes, sir. I don't agree with your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe I will state my statement once again. We agree, and you've just confirmed, that it is in the rules, upon special order they may escort prisoners of war and they may have -- they may have some role to play. But as a given, there's nowhere in the rule that says that the military police has a responsibility for prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If he's going to ask the question that broadly, he needs to give Mr. Butler a chance to review these regulations. But given that, this is getting awfully abstract again, to the point where I think we're wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon. You obviously don't agree with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the question has been asked and answered. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, I'm in agreement, so I suggest you take a more practical view of the matter, not necessarily to please Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll move on to a different area, just to end the matter with respect to the duties and responsibility of the assistant commander for security. I'd like to have the Main Staff instruction in e-court, and that is 2741. It will be at tab 25 in your binder. That will be easier for you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In this document, Mr. Butler, it addresses the relationship with military police and also the technical and management, so we won't cover that. We've done that already. The only part I would like to cover with you is whether, based on this instruction, what type of information, if any, can be withheld from the commander of the brigade. And I refer you, maybe to save some time, to the last part of paragraph 3 and paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, you're asking me a question somewhat by exclusion. It reflects the fact that a security -- members of the security organs must provide to their immediate superiors information and assessments that directly impact the security of their units or institutions. It reflects, you know, also as part of their larger things, that information that doesn't fall into that criteria might not necessarily be shared with the relevant commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, what I'm looking for is your experience, not just to read this instruction, but rather your understanding of the instruction as to what type of information, if any, can the assistant commander for security withhold from his commander.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expect that the information with respect to the operative tasks, interviews related to individuals who might have information on subversive activities by some members of the unit, at least in the early investigative phase -- as I indicated in one of my Prosecution exhibits, an investigation that they were running of a potential threat to General Mladic and other members of the Main Staff, holding open the possibility that brigade commanders or other officers might be part of such a plot, things of that particular nature would be, you know, pieces of information that might not routinely be shared with a unit commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, of course, if the assistant commander for security is investigating in any way into the activities of the brigade commander, then he will keep that confidential at least until conclusions are reached?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, as a matter of practical reality, he would.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And there's always the possibility that the commander may become aware that there was such an investigation, which may be quite detrimental to their relationship; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's a fair statement, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, also from a professional reason, an investigation on one of the other assistant commanders, for example, that would also or could also be kept confidential from the commander, and one of the reasons, based on your experience, I take it you would agree with me, would be not to hurt the other assistant commander until the proper conclusions have been drawn from this investigation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. This is all common sense. We don't need Mr. Butler's opinion for. And if it does refer to -- if he's going to specific facts related to this case, I think it's appropriate that he gets to those facts. Otherwise, it's not relevant, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I disagree with my colleague. He says that we don't need Mr. Butler to comment on a situation like this. On the contrary, I think that if he is to comment or give any expert opinion as to why information can be withheld from the commander, he is in a right position to explain that this can have a detrimental effect and why such information can be withheld.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But do you expect the security officer or assistant commander for security, investigating his own superior, going to his superior and telling him that he's investigating him? So let's move, and I think you can build an argument later on on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I look at this Main Staff instruction, there is a mention here concerning any disciplinary measures which the commander can take against his assistant commander for security. That's in paragraph 5, that's the third bullet. It says here that "He can take disciplinary measures or punitive measures, but that he must first consult with the technical supervisor at the next level," which would be Popovic; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of Drago Nikolic, yes, sir, that would be correct. If Colonel Pandurevic wished to take some form of a disciplinary action against his security officer, he would have to clear that through Colonel Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What's the reason for this, based on your experience?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the practical reason is to prevent a commander from retaliating against a security officer for any variety of reasons. You know, a commander has broad abilities to relieve people or reassign them, you know, as he sees fit, and certainly a commander who thinks he's under investigation for something, you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But let's get away from that scenario. I'm not talking about that scenario at all. I'm talking about any other scenario, other than this one, can the commander still take disciplinary action after consulting the superior technical officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if the superior technical officer concurs with the commander's assessment of the situation and the discipline that he wants to invoke, assuming the technical officer, in this case Colonel Popovic, agrees, the commander can take those actions, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I suggest to you that the reason why it is, according to this instruction, necessary to consult the technical superior, is to ensure that the commander has all the information because he doesn't know everything that the assistant commander for security is doing concerning his operative work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree with that, in so much as, you know, I can foresee a whole set of issues that might arise that a commander might want to take disciplinary action on that would have nothing to do with a professional function, such as a scenario where, again hypothetically, where your security officer is habitually drunk, a situation where he is habitually absent without leave, where his performance or his duty or his behaviour is out of line. Those types of functions would not have anything to do, for the most part, with his professional military responsibilities, but would be within the purviews of his commander to have to take action against.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And his commander, once he confirmed that this has nothing to do with his functions, then he can take those measures?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You're familiar, based on your military experience, of personnel evaluation reports, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am, not only in my own experience but within the VRS experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you're familiar with the fact that within the military and within the VRS, a personnel evaluation report is a "make it or break it," as far as your military career goes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a -- it is a key -- key document with respect to professional officers and their continued career aspirations, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you would not expect somebody who has received an outstanding personnel evaluation report to be someone with whom you have problems with, disciplinary problems or other professional problems?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a superior officer, and in this case a commander, is fairly evaluating his officers with the goal of trying to promote and encourage the best officers for the service and at the same time to take the measures necessary so that substandard performers, you know, don't receive those promotions, yes, he would evaluate them that way, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe my question was not rightly put, but if there is a problem -- if the commander has a problem with an officer, that proper document to put that information in, over and above any disciplinary measures, is in the personnel evaluation report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My last question concerning the management of security officers by the commander is simply: Overall, this instruction here, which was published by the Main Staff under the signature of General Mladic, you've already said that it does not change the application of the JNA rules or doctrine to the security organ, but your professional opinion, did that deprive the commander of any authority or anything with respect to his assistant commander for security?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly does carve in to the limits of authority that the brigade commander has over his assistant commander, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It carves in, but it doesn't prevent him from taking the same actions that he would do against one of his other assistant commanders?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir. I mean, only those areas that were specifically designated as being beyond the authority of the actual commander are those he cannot deal with. Otherwise, the command relationship remains the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I move on to a different topic altogether. But also in your VRS brigade command responsibility report, yesterday you -- sorry, not yesterday, the day before you said that "You did not have a law degree, that you are not an expert on the law of war, like most military officers." Do you recall saying this in response to a question by my colleague?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Most military officers that I know are not -- do not have law degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And are not experts on the law of war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fair, I'll say that they're not experts on the law of war, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you're not either?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, not in that same sense. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in your report, even though you -- this statement you just made, in section 4 of your report, you address issues such as the disciplinary authority of a VRS brigade commander, and you address this topic pursuant to laws and regulations. Now, I quote from your report, where you assess disciplinary authority on the basis of VRS service regulations: "Republika Srpska Law on the Army. Republika Srpska Law on Military Courts," and "Republika Srpska Law on Military Courts, on Courts Martial during a State of War." Now, I submit that you are not qualified to look at these texts and to provide an interpretation that would be of assistance to the Trial Chamber in this case.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would disagree, in so much as that if one looks at this material, it is written in a fairly self-evident manner, and while I don't necessarily hold a law degree, you know, my ability to read and process information, and certainly my ability to, down the line, you know, work with the investigators to interview the individuals within the VRS who had to apply it to ensure that my interpretations were correct, did exist. So, again, my analysis is always conservative, and that's why I extensively document these laws, so that anyone who reads the reports and reads these laws are able to draw their own conclusions, in the event that I don't make the proper conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you reviewed the materials, so it would be my understanding that you read all this -- all those laws, which are written in a plain language, trying to understand what the disciplinary authority of a brigade commander is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe that was crucial with respect to understanding, you know, the authority limits as well as the potential league limits that a brigade commander or even a corps commander would be faced with with respect to his role in ensuring the discipline of his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you try to make a parallel between your experience in the United States Army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. That's why we have about a million lawyers to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you obtain any assistance from the lawyers within the OTP in drafting this part of your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Like I said, my goal was not to find out what our lawyers were saying about it. My goal was to go out, via the investigation, and to find out what the appropriate VRS military prosecutors and military judges were saying about how these were applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So would I be right in saying that in this section, section 4, it is, in your capacity as a former soldier, your layman understanding of this most important topic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is my understand of this topic. And if I'm defined as a layman, so be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, also when I look at section 5 of your report, here you address specifically the relevant national law and military regulations concerning the responsibility of VRS brigade commander. And this specific section of your report deals with the prevention and prosecution of war crimes and crimes against humanity. And just as a reminder, in this section you quote the following: "The order on the application of the Rules of War in the Army of the Serbian Republic ..." At paragraph 5.1, "The interim provisions on the Army of the Republic," "The RS Law on Defence," "The RS Law on the Army," and "The RS Law on the Refugee Care," on the care of refugees. You also address, at paragraph 5.4, guidelines for determining criteria for criminal prosecution and the Criminal Law of the RS for criminal offences against humanity and international law. I will stop here, but the list goes on a bit. Would you agree that you don't have the qualifications which would allow you to provide an interpretation of these laws or regulations or an expert opinion in this regard?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree with that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is your answer the same as before, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer is the same as before, yes, sir. I believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's have the break now. Thank you, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, just when we left before the break, your last answer was that your answer is the same as before with respect to section 5 of your report, which deals with those laws, so I take this to mean that what we find in your report is your layman understanding of these laws and regulations at face value. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have in that section of my report is the laws and regulation as they are stated and my opinion as to how they were being applied within the context of the VRS, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. What I -- I'm interested, nonetheless, in getting your military interpretation of a few or some of these regulations which you refer to in your report. And the first one in this regard is paragraph 7.11 of your report, and that is the RS Criminal Law, Article 239. It's in tab 35 of your binder.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This comes from the Criminal Law, and I can read it for you. I've only included in your tab just this specific Article 239. It's 65 ter 424, page 17 in English and page 104 in B/C/S. This Article 39 reads as follows: "A subordinate shall not be punished if he commits a criminal act by order of a superior officer which relates to official duties, unless the purpose of the order was to commit a war crime or another serious criminal act, or if he knew that the carrying out of the order constituted a criminal offence." I'm interested in your understanding, from a military perspective, of this regulation.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe that it deals with two principles, not necessarily competing, with reflection of command and knowledge. For example, there are other laws, as well as longstanding military practices, where, you know, subordinates, you know, are required to comply with the orders of their superiors. As a broad military function, no military can deal successfully with a fact where subordinates are frequently or constantly challenging either the authority or responsibility of the superiors to give those orders. Particularly with respect to official duties, it is the right of the subordinate to take and accept any order and believe that it is given to him lawfully, just like it's also a collateral obligation for the superior who gives that order to him to have the requisite competence and authority to give that order. However, it also reflects the fact that merely following out orders with respect to war crimes is not a defence. It reflects the fact that under international law, that -- and it has been codified obviously in SFRY law as well as military regulations, reflects the fact that subordinates have a responsibility not to follow orders which they believe are patently unlawful at face value. So that is how I interpret Article 239.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can help you to be a little more precise with the exact text that is before you, would that mean that if a soldier abides or executes an order of his superior, he will not be punished unless the order was a specific order to commit a crime - that would be the first scenario - or the second scenario, if it was obvious that by carrying out the order, a crime would be committed. Would you agree with this interpretation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And, again, the issue would be the specific knowledge of the act. And maybe it's easiest to explain it by analogy. An artillery unit firing at a specific grid location, when its undertaking its military mission, you know, has a right to expect that the coordinates given to it correspond to a legitimate military target. They have no way of knowing whether it does or not. They assume that. And if it turns out afterwards that, in fact, the coordinates were given to a hospital, I mean, at face value a war crime has occurred. The fact that the subordinates do not have knowledge of the criminal target in that respect, you know, they have the right to assume that those orders were given -- well, those orders were given under proper authority. They don't have that specific intent. Conversely, when you're given -- as a soldier, you're given an order to execute a wounded prisoner of war, in most aspects of societies that have militaries, that's going to be recognised at face value as an inherently unlawful act. So, I mean, that's perhaps the best way I can explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to the next provision I'd like to have your opinion on, and that was Article 22 of the regulations on the application of the rules of International Law of War in the Armed Forces of the SFRY, quoted in your report at paragraph 7.11. And Article 22, if I have it, 65 ter 409, page 15 in English, page 16 in B/C/S, and tab 36, Mr. Butler, in your binder.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Again, I only included in this in your binder Article 22, which I am interested in, which I will quote for you: "Responsibility for violations of the laws of war committed on orders. A member of the armed forces shall be liable to criminal punishment also for violations of the laws of war committed by following orders resulting in the commission of a war crime or other grave criminal offence, if he knew that the orders were intended to bring about a violation of the laws of war which constitutes a criminal offence." What is your interpretation, from a military perspective, of this article?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I mean, in this context, being a military regulation, and why I like it, is it doesn't leave much room for interpretation. It means wait says.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move, Mr. Bourgon, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd also -- Mr. President, I will move on, because you're telling me to move on, but I disagree with my colleague that this has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, would you agree with me that this highlights the fact that if a superior gives an order which the subordinate knows was intended to bring about a crime, it constitutes a criminal offence? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It says specifically if he knew that the orders were intended to bring about a violation of the law of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my last question in this regard is: On the basis of your understanding, from a military perspective, of both articles we just saw -- I mean, we have just seen, can we conclude that officers and members of the VRS had the obligation to refuse to follow an order which was understood to be or bring about a violation of the law of war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that under their rules and regulations, that is in fact correct, they were required to not follow that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on to a different topic, which is the levels of land warfare on which you testified about at pages 19581 to 19583. You have defined these levels as being: Strategic, operational, and tactical levels; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Based on your experience, can you confirm the fundamental importance of understanding these levels of war in respect of the planning and conduct of military combat activities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. With respect primarily with my background in the operational and tactical level, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we look at the VRS brigade rules or at brigade level, can you confirm that the rules define a brigade as being a higher combined tactical unit whose components may vary?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe under the JNA and VRS doctrine, a brigade is what's called a tactical formation, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Brigade subordinate units, such as battalions and companies, other than in an exceptional circumstances, would be then considered as tactical units also?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that when we compare these three levels of warfare, the strategic level drives the operational level, which in turn drives the tactical level?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at the tactical level, commanders are given specific combat tasks that they will achieve within a short time frame, and I believe you stated in your examination-in-chief normally not exceeding 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, that's the goal, is that brigades are usually, where they can, in a conventional environment, given tasks that they can accomplish within the 48- 72-hour -- or 48 hours, because in a high-intensity environment, or even in sharp medium-intensity environment, at the end of a 48-hour engagement, the unit is usually at the point where needs substantial resupply and replenishment. Now obviously, in the context of the VRS and in a much static environment, those time frames didn't normally apply with respect to employment of entire units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
