utterances.text: And you would agree that tasks which are assigned to tactical units fit into the operational plan and objectives design at a higher level?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's -- that's how it's supposed to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And based on your experience, would you also agree that it is not always easy to determine where a combat task at the tactical level fits within the operational battle plan?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree with that, in so much as that under a normal practice, before the brigades or the lower formations are going to be constructing their particular battle plans, that they would have some knowledge or appreciation of what the larger or the higher headquarter's plan was. You don't do those in isolation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me give you an example to make things easier for you. A commander who is given the tactical task to take a hill, where he knows that he will lose half of his brigade, may have trouble understanding the overall contribution of taking that hill to the operational plan; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I would expect that a brigade commander, under those circumstances, would have a fairly good understanding of what the overall operational objectives were, particularly given the expectations of his unit's sacrifice. In that respect, I would disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you never commanded troops yourself, Mr. Butler, have you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this level, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And not even at a lower level?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Detachment level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you've never commanded a battalion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You've never commanded forces in wartime, have you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that regardless of their understanding of the -- of the tasks they are assigned, commanders who work at the tactical level are expected to focus on the task they are given, whether or not they understand their contribution to the operational objectives?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are three echelons of -- or four, if you count platoon leaders, echelons of command at the tactical level. I would agree with your analysis in the case of platoon or company commanders. I would not agree with your analysis in the case of battalion or brigade commanders. Those higher commanders are expected to have a broader perspective of what they're doing and why.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But it would not be surprising for officers who worked at lower tactical units, especially battalions and companies, not to understand or be fully informed of the operational objectives of the corps or the Main Staff, for example?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree with respect to the operational objectives of the Main Staff. The corps, it may be a case-by-case basis. I think with respect to -- a good example may very well be the Krivaja-95 op. plan, where the tactical battalion commanders did have appreciations of what the larger-level operational objectives were in this particular case. So, like I say, at that level it's a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this case, to look at the Krivaja-95 operation itself, the battalion commanders were in fact brigade commanders who had assigned themselves as battalion commanders; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, each tactical group had two battle groups associated. That would be the appreciation of the individuals I'm talking about, those battle group commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And officers who worked, Mr. Butler, at the tactical level, they're not likely to have input on the adoption of operational objectives, nor on the planning of combat activities at the operational level; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that commanders at the tactical levels would probably not likely have input as to the operational objectives. They certainly would have input with respect to their opinions as to whether or not their particular units were capable of achieving the missions that they were -- being given to them. As a matter of broader military command and staff, you're not -- as a higher headquarters, you're not going to give tasks to lower formations without an appreciation whether or not they have the resources or material ability to accomplish those tasks. The only way that the higher commands and staffs know that is from the input of their subordinate commanders, who will give them that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But I think we're off on the right track. I was talking about the setting of operational -- of operational objectives or the setting of strategic objectives.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, in that context, certainly company and battalion commanders would not be expected to play a role in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I look at the situation of Drago Nikolic himself as a second lieutenant working in the security organ of a tactical unit, would I be right in saying that you do not expect him to have an input into the setting of operational or strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I wouldn't expect a second lieutenant in the security branch, at a brigade headquarters, to be engaged in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you cannot assume, unless you have evidence to the contrary, that he was aware or that he understood and he adhered to the operational and strategic objectives of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I impart no knowledge of operational directives to that particular individual. I have no information one way or another, so I don't make that assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you could not -- you can't assume, based on what you know of him, that he was aware of these things?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, the normal process that would have occurred is that the relevant portions that he would have needed to be aware of would have gone down separate security channels in that respect, but would -- you know, would they have hand-delivered a copy of an operational directive to him in its entirety? I would say that would be unlikely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move to a different topic, which is basically the scope and aim of your narrative. This was covered by -- in your examination-in-chief, and I'd like to go a bit deeper in these things. You mentioned, at page 19587, that the first aim or the first task you were assigned was to engage in the study of the military and armed forces apparatus that was believed to be responsible for the crime base, in which case that would be the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska, to understand their doctrine and how they would have engaged in operations. That was your first task; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this -- the information or your conclusions in this regard, we would find those in your VRS brigade command responsibility report, corps responsibility report, and Main Staff report; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that your conclusions in your other reports, and I refer here to your narrative and your revised narrative, are of a completely different nature?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusions in the narratives deal with issues with respect to linkage of military units or specific military personalities to the known crime base, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you agree that the conclusions are completely different in your narrative and revised narrative than what we find in the other three reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I disagree, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where has it been asked and answered, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The same question was asked, Mr. Butler gave an answer. This is, I think, about the fourth time that we've talked about this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, it's an objection in the abstract, but it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Butler, we've established and you've already testified that you're not either a criminal law expert, a law of war expert, and what I'd like to turn to is how -- or the modus operandi of drafting this narrative of yours. Explain to us how it worked in the Office of the Prosecution on a day-to-day basis for the years that you were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I were the witness, I would ask you to clarify the question. I don't understand it, to be honest with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will clarify the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I look at -- let's take it from a different angle. Your narrative was drafted for the specific purpose of the Krstic trial; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then explain to us, what was the purpose exactly of your Srebrenica narrative?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initial purpose of the narrative, particularly in the draft forms, was to create a knowledge base for the team's investigators, as well as the Prosecutors with respect to the teams, to get an appreciation and understanding of the military formations that we believed, based on the documents that were coming out of searches, that had a role with respect to the crime base. As you might expect, this knowledge base increases over a point of time. In 1997, when I first arrived here, the Drina Corps was nothing more than an abstract name. It was not defined, it did not have real estate, very few names were associated with it. And as -- you know, as a tool of the investigative process, you know, it would make it very hard for investigators to be able to go out and ask informed questions of witnesses. So the initial goals of the narrative were to provide for the Office of the Prosecutor that specific knowledge base so that they would be able to more effectively conduct their investigative activities with respect to the crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in your -- in your Srebrenica narrative, you say that the original version of the narrative dealt exclusively with the case of the Prosecution versus Krstic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. At a point in time after the indictment and arrest of General Krstic, there was discussion on finalising the particular narrative product for the purpose of using it as a potential Prosecution exhibit. The key issue and in my mind is that, you know, the product in draft forms, it was always a living document for the benefit of the investigative staff dealing with this. It was not a product that was created from scratch post-indictment or pre-trial in any circumstance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you were working in the Office of the Prosecution, preparing this report, you stated in your examination-in-chief that you initially were a member of the military analysis team; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and throughout my entire tenure with the OTP I was with the military analysts team.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the role of those people who work in the MAT, military analysis team, is to provide advice to the people who were preparing these cases?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We advised the investigators and the lawyers who are preparing these cases, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because most of these lawyers don't have a clue of the military, and you're there to assist them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really glad you said that and not me, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is that true or is that not true?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, in reality, you know, one of the reasons why my - not personal presence - but why people of my calibre were invited to come to the Office of the Prosecutor was simply because they did recognise that legal professionals and investigators didn't necessarily have the scope of military background and -- that we would as professional military officers, and that absence was adversely impacting their investigative activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I suggest to you that initially the plan was for them, "them," them being the lawyers and the prosecutors to go to you, but in your case the relationship was reversed and you went to them and you told them how this investigation would be conducted. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within a refined avenue. I'm not sure how it works in other militaries, but in the United States military, intelligence is a customer service enterprise. We are expected and trained to be able to push information to our relevant commanders. In the context that I was working, you know, the investigative team and the lawyers therein were my designated commanders. I would provide intelligence product to them in the form of my analysis and opinions, and I would make recommendations as to avenues that I felt the investigators should pursue with respect to individual -- well, not only individuals, but areas that we wanted to be able to confirm or deny not only with respect to military issues but crime base issues. So in that respect, you know, I had the lane I was responsible for, and I walked down it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So if I try to portray this, you were an investigator with special knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I was a military analyst who assisted the investigators. I was not an investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But when you were determining avenues of investigation, you were actually acting as an investigator?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. You know, what we call Mr. Butler at this point is really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. McCloskey. Let's move, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at page 19588, you stated that "The second component was to do the analysis necessary to identify and place the military units on the ground at the time so that the investigation had determined that crimes had occurred, but the aim was to start making it to the next step, which is to determine who the leaders in those units were and whether or not they would have any potential criminal culpability for the acts." That's what you did with the investigators and the prosecutors in the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, in a broad sense, that was the role I performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So along with the investigators and legal personnel, you look at all the material that was available to them and you made a call whether such material was relevant or no to determine the culpability of individuals?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, yes. As an all-source intelligence analyst, I was looking at all measures of information, and the results of the investigative process, you know, were a form of information that I would take into account. I would identify, as part of my military analysis, those individuals who held either command positions or whom the investigation had identified personal presence at locations, and figure out where they fit within the structure of the militaries. As for an issue of culpability, implying that, you know, I was the one who determined which commanders were responsible and which ones should be indicted or not, you know, again, you know, while I may have a voice on the table on that regard with respect to my opinion, based on my military background, I don't get a vote, and those decisions were made by the career investigators and the career prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in making those calls and by -- in order for you to have a voice at the table, you reviewed that material and you selected which material was relevant for the purpose of establishing culpability?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not exactly. I mean, not even close. I mean, I reviewed the material with respect to laying out the broad framework of the events on the ground, what happened, and what military units were at those locations at times, and the events before and after. Obviously, as part of an indictment review process, you know, my analysts did assemble documents that would be used to support legal aspects that were required to determine whether or not an individual could be indicted and under what mode of liability. So, I mean, we gathered documents, in the case of Colonel Pandurevic, since he is indicted under a theory of superior responsibility as well. You know, we would gather documents and present them which reflect that Colonel Pandurevic, during the time in question, was the commander of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you participated in the selection of these documents, and the documents which are used in your narrative are the result of this selection that you made?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you would agree with me that since you first began in this field, a lot of documents have been acquired or obtained by the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In your revised narrative, and I look at the date here, which was published on the 1st of November, 2002, you state specifically that there was a necessity to update your conclusions in the first narrative because of information coming in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So between the publication of your first Srebrenica narrative and the publication of the second Srebrenica narrative, you considered many additional sources of, if I can use the term, evidence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I considered the new information that we were receiving. I mean, I wouldn't qualify it as evidence. I just considered, you know, all of the new information that we were receiving to determine where it fit into the -- the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that was according to what you say in the introduction to your revised narrative, this was meant to service specifically the trial of Blagojevic, Nikolic, Obrenovic, and Jokic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that was done in -- your report was published on 1 November 2002, at a time when that trial had already begun?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To be precise, you're talking of Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record. I knew that, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, here we are in 2007 [sic], and would I be correct in saying that your narrative has not been updated in the same manner that it was updated for the Blagojevic trial, and it was not updated for this trial in the same manner?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So we can say that your narrative is quite out of date concerning the numerous documents obtained by the Prosecution since your 2002 report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, there's been a five-year lag in the last time that I have worked to revise that. That's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I say that you testified that you in response to a question by my colleague, you said that of course you have a day job, and despite the understanding that you continue to service the Office of the Prosecution as an expert, that there was no way you could have the necessary time to analyse all the new information with a view to producing an updated report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, with a view to producing an updated report is correct. I did, at various points of time, come over and look at the new information primarily to ensure that the new information that was being generated, particularly from the Drina Corps collection, you know, reflected the work of my older products, the narrative -- revised narrative, and in cases where new information would come out that would have to be addressed, would we do that at a testimony state. So, you know, in that respect, I've been reviewing it, but, no, there was not an intention on my part to ever physically re-revise the narrative, to update it at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And anyone who wants to use this report today, in order to apply it to this trial, would necessarily have to take all the new documents that came in since and to try and update your conclusions in order to have a product that could be useful?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, within the context, yes, sir. I mean, but that's the whole point of doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's not -- that's not a criticism on you at all. It's just a fact that this report is five years old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Bourgon, because the last part of your question could have multiple meanings. You said "and try to update your conclusions in order to have a product that could be useful?" I would take it that there are areas that do not need any revision at all, and therefore the report would be useful. There are areas where the update would just confirm what the report contains, and therefore the report will remain useful. And then there may be areas - I'm sure there are - where an update would alter the conclusions that Mr. Butler would have reached in his last report. And unless he's testified about those, then obviously one has to assess what weight to give to his report in relation to those areas. So let's be precise. In other words, the way you put the question would mean that since -- if one does not review all the new documents, then the conclusions reached by the witness in his reports are absolutely useless. This is how -- if you read the question, this is what it says, what it implies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But that's certainly our position, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm telling you this so that you know also that we don't consider you -- at least I don't consider your question to be a fair question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, you are aware that -- you already said that a number of new documents have been obtained by the Office of the Prosecution. Would you agree with me that the documents obtained impact on every single aspect of your report because they were from the Drina Corps collection and it touches upon everything; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would believe -- or I would concur that they are relevant. In many cases, they would not impact the report because they are -- in some cases, they're the identical documents, or in other cases, they're just larger collections of documents which serve to confirm an earlier analysis that I've conducted. So while every document is obviously important, whether it's relevant or whether it would change my conclusions is a case-by-case issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's it, you don't know that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't know the unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The new documents might infirm and might confirm, but you don't know until you look at all the new documents along with your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in the perfect world I would have the several years necessary to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In the -- with respect to documents, are you aware of the fact that you have used a lot of documents in your narrative and that you have testified, both in this trial and previous trial, to a number of documents which have not been presented to any witness in court; are you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular Trial Chamber or in --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In both. Let's take this one here.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that fairly because I have not followed the day-to-day proceedings, so I don't know what has or has not been presented to other witnesses, sir. I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Fair enough, that was my question, whether you knew that, because that's something I can use later in argument, but it was important for me to establish whether you were aware of this fact. But you will agree with me, nonetheless, that if a witness has drafted a document -- if somebody was involved in drafting a particular document, he would be in a better position than you are to comment on the document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point, with all these abstractions and hypotheticals not based on any fact, I'm going to object. I think it's time for the counsel to put his money where these questions are. If he's got documents, if he's got specifics, let's hit them up. We've been going for two and a half hours. Most of what he said has been material that I don't disagree with, that Mr. Butler has already testified to. But if he's got some material, let's put his case to the witness. Otherwise, we're going nowhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, in addition, what's even more important than what you said, Mr. McCloskey, not to diminish the importance of what you said, what is important is: Isn't it a natural conclusion to draw, that the person who draws up a document knows more about it and can testify more about it than a person -- an outsider who is looking at it, even if he is the best of military experts, which I am sure Mr. Butler would concede he isn't? Let's move, Mr. Bourgon. I mean, I think I've made my point clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I'd like to move on to the topic of intercepts. Would I be right in saying that -- you answered some questions in this regard concerning the validity of the intercepts, and you said that initially you had your own doubts about the validity of these -- of this material; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My default position, when the Office of the Prosecutor first identified this material, is that, you know, it might very well be a scope of deception and that it would be, at least from my perspective -- I would look at it very harshly in that light.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now if I look at -- you're aware that there was this intercept project that was conducted within the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What was your role in the intercept project?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My role in the intercept project was limited because of my lack of language skills in that regard, obviously. What my military analysts and I did was that when information would come up in the context of a discussion or a topic, where we felt that we could go back to a Zvornik Brigade or a Bratunac Brigade document as a way of potentially corroborating that information, you know, my office did that. But the actual day-to-day project itself was not something I was involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in the intercept project, this is what was attempted, to take ten examples and to see whether there was corroborating material, to see whether there was any reliability to the intercepts. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And, I mean, again like I said, to the extent that military documents were used to corroborate those intercepts, myself or my analysts were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you, yourself, used the intercepts, did you every time look at this type of exercise to determine the reliability of the intercept or did you simply say, "The intercept project has concluded they're reliable" and they're all reliable?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. What I did as part of my own analytical practice was that until the intercept project, as it were, you know, had completed the -- a month worth of the intercepts, and the month that I directed was 1 to 30 July, I didn't look at them from an analytical perspective. What I wanted to do is I did not want to fall into a trap where I was looking at each individual intercept in or out of context and then somehow finding a way to rationalise that it did or didn't fit. What I wanted to do, from an analytical perspective, was to look at the entire 30-day block, overlay that on the military activities that we understood to occur over that same 30-day block, from the military documents of Zvornik and Bratunac, and essentially see if it fit. I mean, that's the first test of determining whether or not you're a victim of deception. In the broader context of reality as you understand it, if you're a victim of a deception plan, that deception plan becomes self-evident really fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And once --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it fits, it's your first indicator that you're looking at authentic information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's your first indicator. And then would I be right in saying that from that moment on, whenever you quoted an intercept in your report, you took the information on the intercept, including the date, the names and the content, at face value. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was included in my intercept, I was satisfied that I could take it at face value, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The other part I'd like to go through with you is the use of witness information. You testified that you tried to stay away from witness information into this report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you gave the reason that there might have been cross-examination conducted at a later time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I mean, in a military world, I obviously would have included human information, which witness statements would fall under, as part of my all-source analysis, again with a caveat that I would do my job to be able to either verify or refute what was being said. Now, I did obviously have to make an allowance for the fact that, you know, now I don't live in a military world now, I'm living in a legal one, and that that particular role was not mine, it belonged to the triers of fact. So it is a known artificiality of my narrative reports that I make up front, that, you know, I don't wish to try and completely wrap in the human aspect of the information, because that is essentially why this Court exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you -- at the beginning I can understand that, of course, witness information might draw you on a tangent concerning your report, but what happens if information is confirmed in a trial, accepted and put into a judgement, that comes from a witness, then would I be right if this information contradicts your conclusion, that it does invalidate your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, and the reason why I say that is, again, living in a legal world and having to go through a second trial, it was quite apparent, legally speaking, that whatever factual conclusions or legal conclusions that the Krstic trial came to, the Blagojevic Trial Chamber was not only not bound by them, as whether or not they were factually correct, but certainly Defence counsel wasn't going to accept that as well. So as a result, you know, while the Krstic Trial Chamber made its various findings and everything else, for the purpose of my analytical product, you know, I could not take those as confirmed fact that they were in fact the case, and conversely analysis or judgements that the Judges made, I could not take that as confirmed fact for the purpose of my analysis that they weren't true. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So how did you decide when and -- to take witness information in and when not to take information in, in your report? How did you make that call?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in situations, as I've used a witness testimony, only when the description of a crime scene from a witness was necessary just to set the context by which the military was involved around. And maybe the best way to explain that is that, you know, I had to use the statement, and I guess later the testimony in the second case, you know, of survivors from the Orahovac execution site because they were the ones who established a location of a school, they were the ones who established the location of the killing field. They don't -- you know, they don't establish which military units may or may not have been around or who or who did not do anything. So I used the witness statement to establish that particular context in time so that my subsequent analysis with respect to where particular military units were, where particular vehicles were located, what particular individuals were talking about in conversations, made some sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when this information changes in time with the witnesses that you use in your report, and their information changes over time because of cross-examination in further trials, don't you think that this is something that you should have revised in order to update your report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's so broad and abstract.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And apart from that, I mean, did he have the task of updating his report?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, whether or not he had the task of updating his report, what we have now is a report that has not been updated, and we can draw conclusions from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what you have, and you deal with that. I mean, of course you can confront the witness with what you are confronting him with, arguments and all that, but basically I don't think you can assume that it was the responsibility of the witness to prepare an updated report based on everything that you are mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will rephrase my question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, whether or not it was your responsibility, the consequences of this report not having been reviewed with this kind of information has a bearing on the use that can be made of the report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. The indefinite references in that make the question -- "this," "that," I mean it's so general, it really doesn't help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you be specific, Mr. Bourgon, or skip to your next point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, how many -- are you -- you mentioned that you tried to stay away from witness references. Are you aware of the fact that in your report, in your narrative, the revised narrative, out of 676 footnotes, you've used 74 references to witnesses?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll take your word for the answer, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying you use whenever a witness testimony could assist you in establishing culpability, you would then turn to witness evidence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that you're talking about, what, 12 per cent of the references involved, I would disagree with that. And I think if you've read the context of the report, that would not be a fair characterisation of my use of the witness testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In order for you to be firm with your conclusions in your report, the fact is that it is important to look at the testimony, and your report cannot be read without considering the testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My report is designed to be read to allow, you know, the audience, and the audience in this case being, of course, the legal audience of these Chambers, as a road map to what the military documents are, what the intercepts are, how they fit in within the broader context of what the Court may or may not be looking at, and also to establish the regulatory framework by which the various defendants, you know, conducted their military service or police service within the Republika Srpska at the time the crimes occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you'll agree with me that the regulatory framework you're talking about, that's in your command responsibility report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But in the narrative, you're talking about facts and you're making conclusions of facts based on much more than documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Most of my conclusions are strictly based on the -- my analysis of the documents and the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And your conclusions are of little assistance unless it is considered along with the witness testimony in any given case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question for me to answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I don't think it should be a question for you. Let's move, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the fact, Mr. Butler, that despite the witnesses that were quoted in your revised narrative, there has been 28 new witnesses that are not quoted in your report and have testified in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's directly connected to the ruling of the Court and contrary to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Mr. President, what ruling he's talking about, but I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are quite sure. It's obvious that this line of questions is getting you nowhere, in the sense that these can become arguments and we can deal with your submissions in due course. But the fact that there have been 28 witnesses that have testified, that's got nothing to do with the witness. You can make submissions in relation to his reports and his testimony based on the evidence of other witnesses and other facts that have been collected here during the evidentiary stage, and we can proceed along -- along that line, but not along this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I will ask you one last question in respect of your revised narrative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Certainly, we don't want to stop you if you have got a specific instance that you want to put to the witness and ask him whether, having been told this, he is prepared to revise his assessment or his conclusion, but you need to be specific then, not generic and abstract as you have been so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I -- I take the view that asking the witness to conclude that if there are 28 witnesses that he's not aware of, that have not been considered in drafting a report, that he is in the position to say that his report is not complete. And that is an important argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The report has to be looked at as a concrete piece of evidence, and just like every other piece of evidence. Are you going to tell each witness that has come here, "Your testimony is not complete because other witnesses have testified on the same events, which you haven't commented about"? You can't move along these lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I have one last question for you on your revised narrative, and I simply suggest to you that your revised narrative is, one, the result of selection of evidence, that it is both incomplete and out of date. Do you agree with this statement, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that it is five years old. At this juncture, I have not been shown any information which would tend to make me change my mind that the information in it, as well as the conclusions that I've reached, are no longer relevant. So in that regard, you know, I look at it as so far its durability has survived, unless you're prepared to show me something to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me move on to a different topic, Mr. Butler. The events -- I look now at the contents of your revised narrative, and the first issue I'd like to address in this regard deals with the situation which you describe as having taken place in and around Srebrenica, the enclave, between the 2nd and the 13th of July. The first thing I'd like to look at is 65 ter 107, which is tab 33 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're referring to the Krivaja-95 plan of 2 July 1995, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, we are, 2 July 1995, an order from the commander of the Drina Corps, an order for active combat activities. Is it your military interpretation that the task of the corps at that time was to split apart the Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves and to reduce them to their urban areas?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This area has been gone over repeatedly, especially by Defence counsel who had people somewhat involved in this, and the Prosecution will acknowledge Drago Nikolic is up in Zvornik and is really not involved in any sense that the Prosecution can think of that -- yes, this is a joint criminal enterprise, but this is a question of time and our valuable time spent here. This question has been dealt with over and over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. I assume that this is a prelude to another question, and let's hear the other question, because this he has confirmed already.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is indeed a prelude to many other questions which deal with the events in Potocari. I will move to the question, and depending on the answer, I'll see if I have to go back to the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, based on this order from the Drina Corps, so you're familiar with this order, and based on the subsequent warning order or preparatory order that was issued by the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, so bearing in mind these two orders, from -- and on the basis of your report, you concluded that two courses of actions were taken by the people in the Srebrenica enclave, starting on the evening of 10 July 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. You -- the -- my conclusions with respect of the two courses of action were along the basis of decisions that were made by the Muslim civilian and military officials, meetings on 10 July in Srebrenica. The Krivaja-95 order and the subsequent order you're referring to, I'm assuming you're talking about the Zvornik Brigade operations order, not the Drina Corps preparatory order. I don't know that the decisions that the Muslim leadership made about the column had any basis with what the VRS was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Butler, I will rephrase my question to try and make it more precise.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: According to your analysis, and that is in your report, three things are happening simultaneously on 12 July and the morning of 13 July. I'd like you to confirm that this is your -- a result of your analysis. Firstly, you have the woman and children and older men are being transported by bus to Muslim free territory. That's happening starting the 12th of July, in the morning. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At the same time, the Drina Corps is in the process of assembling military units in the preparation for upcoming combat activities in Zepa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that that's on the 12th of July. That's the 13th of July they're doing that. On the 12th of July, they're sweeping through the Bardera [sic] Triangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the forces being included, whether it is on the 12th or the 13th, your report talks about simultaneous activities on the 12th and the 13th, so I look at the period from the 12th, in the morning, until, let's say, the 13th at noon. And in your report, you say that the -- those forces were being assembled for activities in Zepa, and I would ask you to confirm that according to your analysis, this includes the 1st Tactical Group from the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we have a reference to the report? He's clearly looking at it, and I think it would be helpful given the confusion we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Bourgon, could you help us on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Mr. President, but I don't think there's too much confusion. Those three basic conclusions of his refers to what is happening on the 12th and 13th, but we can go into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow so far, Mr. Butler, or do you need to have more specific reference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think what is being referred to is the three actions that I talk about are the movement of the civilians out of Potocari is one action. I'll -- you know, it's the 12th and the 13th, the 12th -- the sweep through the Bardera [sic] Triangle on the morning of the 13th, the uploading of those units and movement towards Zepa as the second action, and then as the third action would be the military activity related to the Muslim column. So, I mean, those are the three things that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's exactly what I want you to confirm, that those three things are happening simultaneously, and then in the meantime, while this is happening, would I be right in saying that your military analysis has revealed that the Zvornik Brigade, or what was left of it, was doing two things; they were holding the confrontation line facing the 2nd Corps of the ABiH Army, and, secondly, under the command and control of the chief of staff, it was preparing to fight and actually fighting elements of the column which had succeeded in crossing the Konjevic Polje intersection? Is that what the Zvornik Brigade is doing this at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am uncomfortable of giving a broad "yes" or "no" over what are -- a very fluid situation happening over the 12th and 13th of July. Certainly with respect to the first issue, yes, the brigade, over those two-day periods, had a responsibility to maintain the confrontation lines against 2 Corps. However, what the brigade was engaged in during the hours of the 12th of July and what the brigade was engaged in in the hours of 13 July, there were substantial differences, because of course the military situation changed in those intervening 24 hours. So I just want to try and be technically accurate on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in regards of the answer you've just provided and what is happening at that time, and in light of your analysis, you will agree with me that the Zvornik Brigade was not involved in any way in the decision-making, the planning, and the actual transport of the group of women, children and elder men from Potocari to free territory under the control of the 2nd Corps of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I mean, there's no evidence that the Command in Zvornik was involved in that, and at present I have no way of knowing whether the brigade commander -- whether he was or was not involved in that. So, I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The answer to your question is your analysis has revealed that it was not involved; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was involved in so much as the fact that buses and trucks were sent to that unit, from that unit to Potocari, but I have no information that says that the Command of the Zvornik Brigade was instrumental in the decision on moving those individuals, you know, from the Command at Zvornik. I have no information on whether or not Colonel Pandurevic, as the commander of the brigade, had any input or opinion, from where his vantage point was down in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you have not seen any evidence to the contrary, either?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: May I have, please, 65 ter 110, which is tab 11 in your binder. This was one request to provide buses which was sent to the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I ask you to confirm that your understanding, from a military perspective of this order, is that it cannot be concluded in any way that there was any understanding that sending buses was part of any illegal activity.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I mean, there's no indication, from the context of this, that it specifies any unlawful act. I agree, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 377, and that's the duty operations officer logbook for 12 July. This one is not in your -- in your binder. Maybe my friend wants to give you the original. Usually, he does. If not, it's on ERN page, for 12 July -- ERN 5732. That's in English. 377 is the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think the one we are looking at is the one you want, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't have any in front of me, Mr. President, so I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see, it's coming. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Butler, this one is -- was included, I believe, in your binder. Let me just give you the right tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you have the ERN page or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Butler, that you have reviewed this operations duty officer logbook, have you, as part of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I mean, I have in so much as the analysis of it is not included in my narratives because this particular piece of information arrived after it was published, but I have -- I have seen and reviewed this document, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you would agree that, of course, this duty operations officer logbook contains plenty of information which could have been of assistance in drafting your narrative?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had it available, I'm quite sure that it is something that I would have included as a relevant part, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we look at the page which is 5732, if we can have the English also on the left side or just -- the entry here, Mr. Butler, talks about -- it's a message which is communicated to the chief of staff, who is standing at the 7th Battalion, and the message reads as follows: "Eight buses from Drinatrans and two of our buses from military police and four of our trucks are going to Bratunac today." My question is: Would you agree that from this entry and any other entries on the 12th of July, there is no indication here that either the duty officer or any other member of the Zvornik Brigade had any knowledge of illegal activities that they are taking part in by sending buses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't need to hear your objection. Please proceed to your next question, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, you will agree with me that requests which are sent for buses to the Secretariat of Defence of the Ministry in Zvornik, that this is an entity that is completely separate from the Zvornik Brigade; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the Ministry of Defence office is an independent entity from the Zvornik military brigade unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I'd like to have 65 ter 157, and it's tab 37 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you see that this is an order where the Drina Corps is addressing the commands of the Zvornik Brigade as well as the Bratunac Brigade, asking for military police to regulate traffic control at the Konjevic Polje junction? Would you agree with me that from the context of this order, and your analysis of it from a military perspective, that no illegal activity can be deducted from this order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler is not here to comment on whether activity is legal or illegal. Opening up that Pandora's Box opens up redirect into a whole other area which is -- I'm not sure that's where we want to go. "Illegal," I mean that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, my colleague has done it, but I will reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, reformulate the question, and let's hear the next one, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: From a military perspective, Mr. Butler, you look at this order, is there anything that is not in accordance with the doctrine or the rules that you have reviewed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, this is a standard military order. I mean, there's nothing improper about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I mentioned a little earlier that in -- concerning this request, and I'd like to have now 65 ter 322, which is a Zvornik Brigade combat report, and it's 12 July 1995, tab 14 in your binder, and I draw your attention to the second paragraph, where it says: "Primary tasks for the unit," and I ask you, when you analyse this document from a military perspective, can you see anything improper being conducted on the military basis, based on what is reported in this combat report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- this is a normal -- this is a normal combat report with respect to structure, context, and substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I look at the paragraph where it says: "We sent to Bratunac, pursuant to your order, eight buses," and then the following paragraph where it says: "One military police detachment was sent to Konjevic Polje," would the drafter of this document, from your military perspective, be of the view that he was doing anything improper?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's so speculative. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The drafter doesn't mean that he was the person who sent the buses to Bratunac or whatever. The drafter is the drafter. The Drina Corps is the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will rephrase my question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, the -- either the drafter of the document, the sender of this document, or anyone else within the Zvornik Brigade involved in the activities described in these two paragraphs, would anyone have -- be of the view that they were conducting anything improper, from a military perspective?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, you don't need to even spell out the objection. Let's move on, Mr. Bourgon, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to Chapter 6 of your narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In this chapter, Mr. Butler, you deal with detention sites and executions in and around Bratunac Municipality. Or, sorry, maybe one last question with the last -- the last part, which is Chapter 5, and that was the transport or transfer of the women, elderly men, and children from Potocari to the free territory. I would suggest to you that your analysis of the material at your disposal has not revealed any involvement whatsoever on the part of Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I mean, I have no documents or evidence which would suggest that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Moving on to Chapter 6 of your narrative, that's the one where you talk about executions in and around the Bratunac Municipality. Just as a reminder, you address in this -- in this part the assembly and detention of Muslim males in and around Bratunac, and you refer to places such as the hangar, the old school, the buses in front of the Vuk Karadzic school and the old school, the buses and trucks at Vihor, the trucks at other locations in Bratunac, and, finally, trucks at Kravica. Based on your analysis of the facts, you would agree with me that the Zvornik Brigade, nor any of its members, were involved in these events as you describe them in your narrative?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I wouldn't -- I wouldn't make that broad conclusion that no members of the Zvornik Brigade were not potentially involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, tell me which ones, then, and where, and how?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly within the context of geographic proximity, the 8th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade, which is also the 4th Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade, is physically located down there. The activities potentially of the military police at the check-point at Konjevic Polje, which I have -- again from documents, I mean, we know they're present there. What their activities were or were not, I don't know. So, I mean, I can't agree with your blanket statement on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, let's take your answer step by step. The 8th Battalion you're talking about, is it correct that you concluded in your report that on that occasion, the 8th Battalion, which may have belonged to the Zvornik Brigade in some way or having returned there after 19 July, at that time was under the command and control of the Bratunac Brigade? Yes. Is that your conclusion in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree that they're under the command of the Bratunac Brigade. However, you know, I also note that there is information that reflects that there's still a relationship with Zvornik and that, you know, we do have information that reflects that particular unit is still in contact with the Zvornik Brigade with respect to issues on needing ammunition, with respect to issues on needing reinforcements, and even in one case with respect to the notification that they've captured at least one Muslim prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will leave the -- those links to you and to the assessment of the Trial Chamber, but I'll ask you to confirm that that occasion, it is your conclusion that it was under the command and control of the Bratunac Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the battalion was formally commanded by Colonel Blagojevic of the Bratunac Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And concerning the activities of the military police at the Konjevic-Polje intersection, you do not have any information of any wrongdoings of those military police at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the specific military police patrol at that intersection at that time, that would be correct, I don't have any specific information that would show their direct involvement in anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I would rephrase my earlier question. Looking at members of the Zvornik Brigade, excluding the tactical group that was away from the brigade and excluding the 8th Battalion, do you see any involvement from any member of the brigade or the brigade itself in those activities described in Chapter 6 of your narrative?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would we also exclude the various drivers of the vehicles that came from Zvornik as well because most of them were military members? Just to be clear in that context, I mean, vehicles and buses that came down, a number of the drivers were members of the Zvornik Brigade. They were involved in that activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll move on to a different question, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we'll have a break now and also, in the meantime, decide whether you still believe that his report is not useful because of the evidence collected in these five years or whether it is useful. Let's have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I rise at this point, I hope, to aid the administration of the Court. Of course, all these things are your decision, but I'm conscious of the fact you encourage us to cooperate. There appear to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also must concede that you do, most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. There appear to be three current legal issues which are fairly urgent, without necessarily being on fire. They include the new witness who was the subject of the motion yesterday, some issue regarding the next witness, who I will not name, lest there be any protective measures sought for him, and some issues concerning material relating to the DNA witnesses who are coming after that. And these will involve some discussion, and, doing the best we can, we think they will occupy about half an hour of court's time. Now, in that event, and Mr. Nicholls is here to deal with at least one of the issues, we've spoken during the break and we felt it would be more convenient, particularly to Mr. Butler, if we allocated a slot tomorrow to deal with those matters, perhaps first thing in the morning, rather than cause you to stop early tonight and not have enough time to deal with all the issues. So as I say, respectfully, of course, you run the court, but that would be, I think, our joint suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, will you make an effort to finish your cross-examination today?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't think so, Mr. President. I've got two and a half hours done, and I believe I have an hour and a half --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have three hours and 53 minutes, and that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I need an hour and 10 minutes or 9 minutes or whatever to bring it to five hours, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Haynes, and of course I take it that you were representing your colleagues --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We hope so, too. Okay. We'll -- do you wish to say you agree or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We do agree. Well said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll postpone the discussions, which we had in mind to deal with -- to have at the end of this sitting, no matter that you think 30 minutes will be required, to tomorrow morning first thing, so then Mr. Butler comes in after the bit and will continue with the cross-examinations. Okay, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we left off on the issue of whether the Zvornik Brigade was involved in the activities described in Chapter 6 of your narrative, and my next question is the following: Will you agree with me, from a military perspective, that once those -- when the Zvornik Brigade did dispatch buses and trucks as requested by the Drina Corps, that those drivers, at least from a factual point of view when they reported to the person requesting the buses, were under command and control of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in that context I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question deals -- just to finish on Chapter 6 of your narrative, which deals with the issue of these events. Would I be right in saying that your analysis of the information at your disposal did not reveal any participation whatsoever on behalf of Drago Nikolic in either sending buses or sending military police to Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information that he participated in sending buses or sending the military police to Konjevic Polje, yes, sir. That's a fair statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we look at the first two executions which are described in your report, which took place in Cerska as well as Kravica, would it be fair to say that your analysis, from a military perspective, did not reveal any involvement on the part of Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I can make that particular blanket statement for two reasons. The first reason is that, as I note in my narrative on, on 13 July the travels of one military police vehicle do put it in the Kravica area at around the afternoon hours of 13 July. I also am aware of the statements that Milorad Trbic has provided to the Office of the Prosecutor with respect to his presence at that location on 13 July, at the time the executions were occurring or had occurred. So I am aware of those two facts. And, of course, given the relationship between Drago Nikolic and Milorad Trbic, I'm not prepared to make that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, leaving aside Trbic, because he's -- of course, not evidence that we've heard in this case, at least not to this day, but focusing on that vehicle that you're talking about, I'd like to look at 65 ter, which is exactly this -- this vehicle log that you have, 65 ter 136, which is in tab 38. In your Srebrenica narrative, you highlighted the places where this vehicle travelled to.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you say again the tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The tab would be tab 28.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misheard you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, not -- tab 19. And that is 65 ter 904. In your report, Mr. Butler, and that was on page -- the paragraph 7.3 of your report, the Srebrenica narrative, you indicated where the vehicle or the Opel Record that you've just referred to was travelling on 13 July. That's the document that you have in front of you. And from 13 July, we have Standard IKM, Zvornik local, Orahovac, Standard, Bratunac and Zvornik; do you agree with that? Is that what you have in this document which you have in your binder and which is now on e-court for the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: With respect to travelling to Bratunac on that day, I'd like now to turn to 65 ter 136, which is at tab 38. And I suggest to you that this document -- I will ask you to confirm that this document shows that there was a UNHCR convoy that travelled on 13 July from Karakaj to Bratunac. Can you confirm this, from your reading of this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Paragraph 3. Now, we had evidence in this case from a witness that he was driving this car and he accompanied this convoy on this vehicle. In light of this conclusion, if it was to be accepted, would that show that your conclusions of the possible involvement of Zvornik Brigade in those two executions in Cerska and Kravica would not be the same?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I understand that the individual -- I don't know that he's testified and I won't mention his name, because I don't know what the circumstances are, so I don't know what he may or may not have said about that travel. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let's go to the point where --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the witness said that, then certainly for the purpose of escorting the convoy down to Bratunac, that's what he would be doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's what is written there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And on the same document, when you indicated that there was some travel, Standard to IKM, the fact that your investigation has revealed that Drago Nikolic was on duty at the IKM on the 13th of July, could that also be accounted for -- or account for what is indicated, "Standard-IKM," on 13 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And is there any possibility, I say "possibility," that the locations indicated in that vehicle log that you just saw, and we looked at the locations, that on that day the vehicle travelled to those locations for military police business, unrelated to any execution; is that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a possibility with respect to Kravica and, as you said before, potentially Cerska, because I just have no information about that. I don't know whether I hold that as a possibility, as an extension of the travels to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Fine, I accept your conclusion, because I -- we will have evidence to the contrary. But now I'd like to turn to 65 ter 377, which is something that you mentioned during your examination-in-chief. That's the duty officer or duty operations officer logbook. I'd like to have page 16 in English and page 122 in the B/C/S language. And that was for the 13th of July, 1995. And during your examination-in-chief, you referred to a request for a bulldozer, which was addressed to the duty officer of the Zvornik Brigade on 13 July. You recall testifying to that effect?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would simply ask you to look at the duty officer's logbook, which will appear in front of you. I do not have this one in your logbook. From your analysis of the information in the duty officer logbook, where it says: "Bulldozer," is there any possibility to conclude that the person drafting -- or the person or the officer on duty knew what the bulldozer was requested for?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to the term "any possibility." This is a term that helps no one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will rephrase to please my colleague, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I like to please my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, also I'm not seeing -- maybe it's just me, but I'm not seeing "Bulldozer" on the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Oh there, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: From your analysis of this duty officer's logbook, can you conclude where the bulldozer or why the bulldozer is requested?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, again looking at this one specific reference, it's impossible to say why. I mean, I think we've coupled this with the intercept which talks about, you know, requesting the bulldozer, so again I don't look at it in isolation, but from this, there's nothing that would refer that the individual who wrote this down in the log has any indication of why it's being asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that was my next question. The intercept that was coupled with this information, would that allow you, from your military perspective, to determine why the bulldozer was requested?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe I've testified that I believe why the bulldozer was requested. I think what you're looking for, if I understand the line of questioning correctly, is that I don't believe there's anything in the intercept that would give the correspondent who's taking this at Palma an idea of what the bulldozer was being -- or what the bucket loader was being asked for in that respect. They just wanted to know whether it was available or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on to a different topic, which is your -- the events which you review in Chapter 7 of your narrative or revised narrative, and there's only a few questions I'd like to ask you here. You recall that you concluded that "The 4th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade was involved in the planning, detention, execution and subsequent burial at the Orahovac site"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we have a reference to where that's -- that it sounds like a quote is coming from?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Again, I will be happy to please my colleague. At paragraph 7.6 in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I see it on the screen or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And 7.6 -- this is 6. The number of your report was 684, and that was in English on page, I believe it would be, 63, but that's the paragraph 7 -- 7.6. I will read you your conclusion in there, and it says first: "This area falls within the zone of the 4th Battalion of the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade."
