And it goes on to say: "Survivor testimony and documents from the Zvornik Brigade indicate that elements of the brigade command, the Engineer Company, the Military Police Company and elements of at least the 4th Infantry Battalion were all involved in the planning, detention, execution and subsequent burial of Muslim men at the Orahovac site." My question relates specifically to the 4th Battalion. Would I be correct in saying that your conclusion, in respect of the 4th Battalion, rests solely on two things, which is: Survival testimony of someone called Gojko Simic and also the fact that what you refer to, the 4th Battalion or the Orahovac being in the zone of responsibility of the 4th Battalion? I simply suggest to you that you have no other element which suggests that the 4th Battalion was involved in the events in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree, I mean, and certainly contemporary interviews with not only members of the Command of the 4th Battalion as well as members of the Command of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade note that soldiers from the 4th Battalion were directed to go to that location in order to guard prisoners there that were getting out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will make my question more precise. I was talking about the -- the killings in Orahovac, and is it your conclusion that in respect of the killings in Orahovac, other than for the survivor testimony of Gojko Simic, that is your sole source of information to say that they were involved in the killings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mean the killings at the meadows, not the schools?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Allegedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Allegedly, the meadows, not the schools?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The killing places where people were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. There were different places. If we could be specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In Orahovac, Mr. President, and there's only one killing zone with two places, and that was Lezete 1 and Lezete 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: People died at the school in our case, and that's a clear part of our case, so we need to be specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to be specific, Mr. Bourgon, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm referring to Lezete 1 and Lezete 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Those are terms you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, with respect that Gojko Simic was an individual who was identified by a witness, and who we were able to corroborate was a member of that particular unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my question is: In addition to that, you have no other source of the involvement of members of the 4th Battalion in the executions in Lezete 1 and Lezete 2?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would actually like to go back to my report on that, because my memory is unclear as to whether or not I identified a vehicle associated with the 4th Battalion that I believed was moving people back and forth to the school. I mean, it may be I'm confusing it with the 6th or 7th Battalion, but I believe that there is a reference in my report. If there isn't, then I am confusing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then I will look at your report and get back -- and we will come back on this point a little later. One of the issues that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you let him have his report in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We're trying to have the report up on the screen, but I do not have a hard copy with me, other than one that is highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That would be an excellent idea. I mean, we can try to go track one down. But given the degree of these questions, it would be best if he had a hard copy, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I can move on to a different issue, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next issue, Mr. Butler, deals with the decision to move the prisoners in the area of the Zvornik Municipality. Would you agree that whoever made that decision, on the basis of your military expertise, that sending the prisoners in the same geographical area where the column was heading, with a view to joining forces with the 2nd Corps of the ABiH, makes very little sense from a military perspective?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- in the first view, working under the assumption that the actual movement and execution of the prisoners in the Zvornik Brigade made any sense whatsoever from a military perspective, the decisions may well have been made with respect to the fact that they were still underestimating the size and the threat posed by the column. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, that was my next question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that may very well have been one of the thought processes behind why they would be safer -- or why Zvornik would be a more suitable location than keeping them in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me begin, then, by saying: Looking at the risks associated with such a decision, it would be possible -- it would not be sound, from a military perspective, because prisoners might escape and attack the population? Would that be a fair risk that could happen if you have the two in the same area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, in the abstract, it's a risk. However, when you look at the context of what was happening in Bratunac, where the civilians were jammed into structures in the heart of the town, there was certainly less risk to the civilian population under that context of storing them in schools away from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I'm not talking about the abstract, I'm talking about the concrete, I'm not -- and the situation is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't argue with the witness. Go to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm making my question more precise, not dealing with an abstract situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't argue with him, please. Go to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did your analysis of these events reveal the possibility -- not the possibility, reveal that the presence of prisoners in the municipality of Zvornik and other close municipalities made the soldiers very nervous on the line, and some of them actually wanted to go and protect their families? Are you familiar with that? You can answer by "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- it's a broad -- it's a broad statement, and I think there -- I'm just trying to -- I know there was a general awareness among the [indiscernible] of the soldiers that their families were in some form of threat. I -- most of that threat was related to the column. I'm not aware of -- I'm not aware of information going forth that in places like Pilica -- I'm just not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me move on, Mr. Butler. Are there risks associated with placing the column and the prisoners in the same geographical area, from a military perspective? Please answer "yes" or "no." You may say "no" if you want, but I want to know if it's a sound military decision? That's all I'm asking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. "place the column," I don't think I understand. "Place the column," how do you place the column anywhere? You can fight the column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I like to please my colleague, but enough is enough. My question is quite clear. Mr. Butler knows exactly which column I'm talking about, and the fact that they decide to bring the prisoners in the Zvornik area while that column is going on, Mr. Butler knows what I'm talking about, and he can answer "yes" or "no," whether this is a sound military decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If that is the question, it's been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you understood the question, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I think I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then can you answer it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, with respect to risk, you know, the decision to move the prisoners up to the Zvornik Municipality, in the broad sense, did represent an acknowledgment that there was some risk involved. They had to get them out of Bratunac. They were directed to do so. They assumed a risk there. They marginalised that risk. There was far less risk dealing with detention centres in places like Pilica and Rocevic and even the Petkovski school that were far removed by terrain and distance from the fact that the column could potentially reach them and liberate the prisoners. As a matter of the school of Orahovac, that is probably the closest place where there was an assumption of risk, because it's the closest point of approach between a known holding and detention facility and the column. But I think if I noted in my analysis that, you know, at best there was a three-kilometre separation, so, you know, while it was an acceptance of risk, in part, to make this decision, in light of the alternatives that were happening in Bratunac, someone apparently made the decision that the risk was acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You can confirm, Mr. Butler, that you concluded in your report that whoever decided to send the prisoners to the Zvornik area was not someone from the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents and intercepts that I have don't reflect that. I can't make that conclusion as a broad statement because I don't know whether Colonel Pandurevic was or was not involved in that decision process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If he has a specific reference to a conclusion, he's incumbent, in asking that question, to direct Mr. Butler to it. He said he concluded that in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll move on to a different topic, Mr. President. I do have a reference in Chapter 9, and I will bring it to the witness when I conclude my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: For now, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A brief objection, Your Honour, to going to one area and then bouncing away and then bouncing back. This takes an incredible amount of time and is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he is Canadian, not Australian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I won't repeat what my colleague said. Depending on the number of objections, I'll know when I'll complete my cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's being suggested that you abandon the kangaroo tactic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, you said earlier on that one of the reasons they decided to bring the prisoners in the area of the Zvornik Municipality might have been because they had wrong information on the column; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, what I -- the question was whether there was risk involved. I don't know whether they had -- I mean, they knew about the column, obviously. Whether -- you know, whether that was a factor, you know, I don't know. But you didn't ask me whether they were -- because they had wrong information and that's the reason why they did it. I don't know why they did it. The information that we have, with respect to the broader context, is that there was a decision that they had to be taken out of the Bratunac area. Was that the sole driver behind the decision? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me read your answer here, and that was on page 93. Your answer was: "In the first view, working under the assumption that the actual movement and execution of the prisoners in the Zvornik Brigade made any sense whatsoever from a military perspective, the decisions may well have been made with respect to the fact that they were still underestimating the size and the threat posed by the column." Is that an answer that you gave me; "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I don't believe that's inconsistent with what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I suggest to you that one of the reasons why the prisoners might have been sent to Zvornik is because when they were sent there, there was no intention to kill and it was the closest place to the exchange area. Would that be, in your evaluation from a military perspective, a possibility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go to your next question, Mr. Bourgon. You can't expect the witness to testify on the intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Butler, that the Zvornik Municipality was the closest area where, if an exchange was to be organised, the prisoners should have been -- should be placed there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree. And given the fact that the civilians were being led out of the area under the control of the Vlasenica Brigade, if proximity to the confrontation lines was the sole driving criteria, it would have made sense to bring them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We'll get somebody else to counter what you say, so I accept -- I accept your answer. I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, Mr. McCloskey, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to move to a different topic, which is tactical intercepts. Are you familiar with the fact that tactical intercepts were obtained by the Office of the Prosecution? And I'm referring to the intercept of VHF radio communications.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are you aware when this material was obtained, and was it considered in producing your revised narrative?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I'm aware when it was generally received, which I believe was roughly a year or 18 months after the multichannel intercepts. I don't believe, and I have noted in my narrative, I don't believe I that I had relied on them, because I don't think at the time that I was convinced that they were fully -- had been fully authenticated. I mean, that's how I recall, and I think I've said that in my narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: May I go to 65 ter 2232, which is the tactical intercepts, and you can find them in tab 24 of your binder. I'd like to go to page 5 in English, and the top part where it says: "1800 hours." And we're talking about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you have it with you in your binder?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it -- oh, which page in the English or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Page 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Yes, sir, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You see where it says: "1800 hours. The road to Crni Vrh was closed"? At the top part.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just a little bit down, it says: "Omega 21 is in Pilica." So you agree with me that Pilica is one of the areas where prisoners were taken; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If Omega 21 is identified as being a member of the MUP, would that be, sir, an important factor that was omitted in your narrative?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, in what context, the fact that there's MUP in Pilica means, you know, they're supposed -- it's a village area. I don't know why there wouldn't be -- I mean, are we talking about a MUP company is deployed, or are we talking about a specific patrol car? And that's why I always hate to use on the tacticals, because some of these are just so abstract that it's difficult to put a meaning to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you say today you're of the opinion, that as the Prosecution's expert, we should not consider these tactical intercepts; is that what you say, that they're not reliable?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, what I'm saying is that I have not -- because the reliability hasn't been established to me because they were, I assume, authenticated before, or after I arrived, or after I left, I didn't rely on them. If the Court does rely on them, I presume it will do so in the context of witnesses who have testified as to what they mean, and as well as with the other intercepts, to testify as to the product and process behind that. I'm just not aware of that, so I can take what it says at face value when I can understand what it means, but these -- I don't generally do that with the tactical intercepts, and particularly what you've just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on to a different but related topic, and that is, of course, communications using VHF radio. From your military experience, you would agree that it is the norm for commanders, using radios on the battlefield, to be accompanied by a signalman?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, especially with their radios, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And signalmen would be used, based on your military experience, to receive messages sent to the commander or to transmit a message from the commander to another station?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, their general -- their general function is to manage and operate the radio. I mean, obviously there will be times when the commander will grab the radio, microphone himself, and give direct orders. But, you know, as a general rule, the general practice is that the commander is going to basically tell the radio operator, you know, who he wants to talk to and what message he wants to relay, if it's a short one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And taking you up on what you just answered, which is exactly my point, if two commanders are speaking to one another, on the basis of your experience on the handling of this type of radio, they would not go through their signalman, they would speak directly to each other; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, if they wanted to speak to each other in person about a relatively complex issue, yes, it would make sense that the commanders at both stations spoke personally to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'm not -- whether the issue is complex or not, my question relates to the difficulty in communicating via radio, and if two commanders speak to one another, based on your military experience, they are not likely to go -- to do so through their signalman, but they will speak directly, one on one, using the device themselves; is that your military experience?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's asked and answered, and it's really speculative as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Asked and answered, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm not sure where the answer is and for sure, Mr. President, it's not speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's explained to you that under certain circumstances, the two commanders would speak directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But my question is he's supposed to be a military expert, and I'd like him to say how it works in the practice, in the real world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's told you already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection. You know, a soldier doesn't get in the face of his commander and question his orders, nor should a lawyer to the Judges. You've made your ruling. That should be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Give me a break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Move --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Come on, Mr. -- come on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, you can have a drink together afterwards, but in the meantime, let's proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Final couple of questions before we end today, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Chapter 2 of your revised narrative, you speak about members of the Zvornik Brigade at paragraph 2.8. One of the individuals you refer to is Captain Trbic, and that was on page 20. My sole question is: Did your analysis reveal that before being appointed as assistant to the assistant commander for security in March of 1994, that Trbic was the deputy commander of the 2nd Battalion? Are you aware of this, on the basis of your analysis of the material at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Again, I might have seen a vague reference to that as a -- as a component of my research, but tracking back that far, no, I don't recall that. It may very well be the case, but I just don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On the basis of your military experience, would you agree with me that a battalion commander and his deputy, involved especially in combat activities, are likely to develop a very close relationship?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a lot of human-nature factors involved. I mean, from a professional perspective, a commander and a deputy commander represent the command team, and as a matter of professional ethics and work product and everything else, I mean, they should work very much in harmony with each other. Obviously, you know, people are people, and that may not be the same some time even in war. But certainly from a professional perspective, the battalion commander and a battalion deputy commander ought to work in almost a seamless manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On the -- in this section there is one person that was missed out, a certain Major Galic, who was the assistant chief of staff for personnel. Are you aware of who this individual is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you -- did you consider, when assessing the material at your disposal, the involvement of this individual, Major Galic, in operational matters within the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what context? I mean, in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In July of 1995, is he an individual, based on your analysis of the material at your disposal, who was involved in operational matters?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He -- I can't tell you whether he was or was not. I mean, he may very well have been during some period of that month, you know, as a duty officer at the IKM or as a duty officer at the main headquarters, which would have inserted him into some of the operational issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But it's not an issue that stood out for you, in terms of his involvement into operational matters?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it's not an issue that stood out for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And just again from your military experience, if his name appears on the working map which was in the operations room, as the person who drafted the map, would that be an indicator that this man was at least knowledgeable of operational matters?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it would be an indicator again, depending when the map was drafted and what his state of knowledge was, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's my last question. Tomorrow, I only have one area I'd like to get into, and it is based on a hypothetical scenario which I would like to give to the witness so he can look at it, and tomorrow we'll ask some questions based on this hypothetical scenario, as an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. McCloskey will stay awake all night thinking about possible objections already, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Mr. President, he can do it any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was confused. Is the intent to give me the hypothetical now or tomorrow morning? You know, I thought you had indicated you wanted me to think about it. I don't know what the answer is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no, let's stop, let's stop now. I mean, tomorrow morning we won't start at 9.00 sharp with you because we will have other things to discuss which are unrelated to your testimony, and after we have discussed those, then we'll call you in. Thank you and have a nice evening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 25th day of January, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.02 p.m.,
